Changelog

Source: NEWS.md

zuarrow 0.0.0.9000

  • Initial CRAN submission.

Handles

  • arrow_schema() makes a schema handle from an Arrow format string, from an R object, or from any schema, array or stream handle, and format() and print() show Arrow’s type notation.
  • Handles share the ‘nanoarrow’ package’s layout and inherit from its classes, so handles cross between the two packages without conversion.
  • arrow_validate() runs the bundled ‘nanoarrow’ C library’s validation at "minimal", "default" or "full"; "full" also checks that every string is valid UTF-8.
  • arrow_equal() compares two schemas, arrays or streams, and says why they differ.
  • arrow_metadata() and arrow_metadata<- read and write schema metadata, keeping binary values as raw vectors.
  • zuarrow_info() reports the versions zuarrow is built from.
  • Every error inherits from zuarrow_error, and the lossy warning from zuarrow_warning.
  • An error names the function or S3 method you called, such as arrow_stream() or as.data.frame(), never an internal helper (#124).

Converting to and from R

  • arrow_to_r() converts an array to an R vector and a stream or struct array to a data frame; as.data.frame() and as.vector() do the same, and arrow_next() reads one batch.
  • A conversion is exact or it fails: lossy = "error", the default everywhere, raises zuarrow_lossy_error naming the column, the row and the package that would read it exactly. lossy = "character" gives the values’ exact text, "warn" and "allow" the nearest R type.
  • A column with no values is never lossy: under "error" and "warn" it takes the form "allow" gives, so reading a zero-row result, as dbplyr does for a table’s columns, no longer fails (#177).
  • to names the R type a column must become.
  • Conversion in both directions reads and writes typed buffers in one loop wherever a column has no dictionary or run-end encoding, so most types convert as fast as with nanoarrow or faster, with every exactness check kept.
  • copy = FALSE defers string columns in arrow_to_r(), arrow_next(), arrow_read() and as.data.frame(). Each becomes a character vector that creates its R strings on first use, which is most of the cost of a string column. Values are checked during the conversion either way, so the errors are the same. The default, copy = TRUE, creates every value at once.
  • A deferred string column holds its own reference to the Arrow buffers, so it keeps its strings when the array handle it came from is released, or released and reused. It used to raise zuarrow_handle_error, or, for a reused handle, read freed memory (#181).
  • arrow_array() and arrow_stream() build arrays and streams from R vectors and data frames, checking every value against a given schema. The exact text that lossy = "character" returns is written back as the type its arrow_type attribute names. Only that canonical text is read, so other forms of a value, such as "+1" or "01", and a time of day of 24:00:00 are a zuarrow_lossy_error (#213).
  • A value that would not export exactly is a zuarrow_type_error: a non-ASCII native string with no exact UTF-8 form, as in a C locale (#203); a matrix under a schema that is not a list type, or with a class (#209); a factor with an NA level (#211); a tzone, difftime units or arrow_extension_metadata attribute that is not one valid value (#214).
  • arrow_types() lists the built-in type table.

Nested types, dictionaries and the registry

  • Structs convert to nested data frames, lists of every kind to list columns, fixed-size lists to list columns or, with arrow_matrix(), to matrices, and maps to lists of key/value data frames. Each converts back.
  • Factors convert to and from dictionary<int32, utf8>, ordered factors included; a stream’s batches read as the union of their levels. Other dictionaries and run-end encoded arrays decode to their values.
  • A fixed_size_binary column read as a list of raw vectors keeps its width in arrow_width, and is written back as fixed_size_binary (#210).
  • Extension types keep their name and metadata as attributes and are restored on export; arrow.bool8 reads as logical. Field metadata round-trips through the arrow_field_metadata attribute.
  • arrow_register(), arrow_unregister() and arrow_registry() let a package make a lossy type exact with its own R class, by format string, prefix pattern or extension name, in both directions.
  • A to handler of (array, schema, lossy) receives the caller’s lossy policy, so a registering package applies it to values its class cannot hold. Two-argument handlers work as before. When several keys match, the extension name wins, then the exact format, then the earliest pattern.
  • A prototype of a registered class in to, such as zuint::int128(), converts a column through that registration whatever its Arrow type.
  • A registered extension over a dense_union or sparse_union, such as geoarrow.geometry, reads through its to handler, which receives the union array with its type ids, offsets and children as they are. A union with no handler still fails with a zuarrow_lossy_error (#171).

The IPC file and stream formats

  • arrow_read() reads the Arrow IPC file format (.arrow, Feather version 2) and stream format (.arrows) from a path, a raw vector or a connection, eagerly into a data frame or lazily as a stream, with column selection.
  • arrow_read() also takes a list of IPC streams and reads them as one, as Spark Connect sends a result: one data frame, or with lazy = TRUE one stream. Every stream must have the first one’s schema.
  • LZ4 and zstd bodies are decompressed through ‘zukomp’, so a compressed file opens everywhere; dictionary batches and deltas are applied, and the binary-view, string-view, list-view and run-end-encoded layouts decode.
  • Every message is verified and checked against arrow_limits() before it is used, and every batch passes full validation, so hostile input is a zuarrow_format_error or zuarrow_limit_error. Big-endian input is refused.
  • Full validation also checks that every binary or string view points inside its buffers, which the bundled C library does not.
  • arrow_write() writes data frames, struct arrays and streams as the Arrow IPC file or stream format, to a path, a connection or a raw vector, in record batches of batch rows.
  • Factors are written as dictionaries, one dictionary batch before the first record batch, or as strings with dictionary = FALSE; schema and field metadata and extension names are kept.
  • compression = "lz4" or "zstd" compresses each buffer through ‘zukomp’, at the codec’s own level; the default is uncompressed, so every reader opens the output.
  • The output is deterministic: the same input gives the same bytes, with no timestamps and every padding byte zeroed.

Fixes

  • A lossy value in a dictionary or run-end encoded column is checked as the rows read it. The zuarrow_lossy_error names its row, and a value that no row reads, or that only null rows read, is not lossy. Before, any such value in the dictionary or the runs raised an error with no row (#107).

  • The zuarrow_lossy_error of a dictionary column names the package that reads its value type exactly, such as ‘zuint’ for int64 values, as a run-end encoded column’s does. It used to look the target up by the index type and name none (#144).

  • arrow_array() refuses a list column of data frames whose elements differ in column names, column order, or a column’s class, type or attributes, with a zuarrow_type_error naming the column. It used to let rbind() coerce an integer column to character. A plain factor column’s levels may still differ; an ordered factor’s may not (#103).

  • arrow_array() refuses a list column of ordered factors whose levels differ, with a zuarrow_type_error. It used to write them as one plain factor with the union of their levels, so they read back unordered. Elements with the same levels still round-trip as ordered factors (#138).

  • arrow_schema() of a registered vector, or of a data frame holding one, takes the type from the whole column, as arrow_array() does. A from handler that picks the type from the values gave the two a different type before (#113).

  • An object goes through the registration of its most specific class: an object of class c("sub", "base") uses the "sub" registration, in arrow_array() and as a prototype in to, whichever loaded first. It used to use the one registered first (#114).

  • A package that registers a pattern again, as on a reload, keeps the pattern’s place among overlapping patterns. It used to move last (#115).

  • arrow_array() of a registered vector is a zuarrow_registry_error when the from handler builds an array of another length, as it is for a data frame column, and a zuarrow_handle_error when the handler returns a released array (#123).

  • An extension whose storage type converts exactly stays exact. An inexact registration for arrow.json or arrow.uuid is refused, and one for another extension name is a zuarrow_registry_error when it would read a column of exact storage under lossy = "warn" or "allow" (#133).

  • A POSIXct round-trips through Arrow under the default policy. Millisecond and microsecond timestamps are exact by value: a value is exact when its double of seconds rounds back to the same integer, and only one that does not is a zuarrow_lossy_error naming its row. Before, every microsecond timestamp was lossy, so zuarrow could not read back what it wrote, and the millisecond bound of 2^53 let a few values past 2^51 through inexactly (#130).

  • arrow_read() applies a delta dictionary batch that extends a dictionary already holding values, for fixed-width, binary and string values. Before, the bundled decoder refused it with a zuarrow_format_error (#81).

  • arrow_write() writes a dictionary of struct or list values with the value type’s children in the schema. Before, the bundled encoder dropped them, so the output could not be read back (#140).

  • arrow_read() bounds what delta dictionaries build. Each delta copies the whole dictionary, so many small deltas could take memory and time quadratic in their number. A dictionary that deltas extend is now held to max_batch_rows values and max_message bytes, and every byte the copies build counts against the new max_dictionary limit of arrow_limits(), 256 MiB by default. Going over one is a zuarrow_limit_error (#101).

  • A stream whose next batch fails raises the same class from every function: a zuarrow_format_error, zuarrow_limit_error or zuarrow_codec_error from zuarrow’s IPC reader, and a zuarrow_handle_error from any other producer. Before, arrow_validate() and arrow_equal() always raised a handle error (#83).

  • A registered from handler is called once on the whole column, and the column takes the type of the array it returns. So a handler may choose the type from the values, as decimal chooses a precision, and arrow_write() and arrow_stream() write the column in batches of that type (#91).

  • A registered from handler that builds a batch whose nested type differs from the column’s, such as list<int32> in a list<int64> column, raises a zuarrow_registry_error. Before, only the top-level format was compared, so the batch’s bytes were read as the wrong type (#100).

  • A zero-row data frame is a stream of one zero-row batch, as it is one zero-row array, so arrow_stream() and arrow_write() keep a factor’s levels, nested ones too. Before, the stream had no batch and the levels were lost (#212).

  • A registered from handler is called once on the whole column for every layout, and each batch is a copy of that array’s rows. Before, a column that was not fixed-width was built again per batch from x[rows], which drops the class and attributes. A sliced run-end encoded column is now written as its rows, not refused (#215).

  • A to handler’s piece for each batch must have that batch’s length, or it is a zuarrow_registry_error naming the batch. Before, only the total was checked, so rows could shift between batches (#216).

  • A to handler’s data frame pieces are combined column by column, and pieces whose class c() drops keep the attributes they share. Pieces whose attributes differ are a zuarrow_registry_error. Before, several batches could give another class or another shape than one batch (#198).

  • A dictionary or run-end encoded column goes to the handler registered for its value type, which receives the decoded values. Before, the handler for the index type received the dictionary, so a dictionary with int64 indices went to an int64 registration and was read wrong, and a dictionary of decimals did not reach decimal’s (#93).

  • A package that registers a key it already owns, as on every reload, does so without a message (#92).

  • A registered from handler that returns a released array raises a zuarrow_handle_error. Before, it raised a base error (#126).

  • arrow_to_r() and arrow_equal() check every offset of an array from another producer before reading it. A string, binary or list offset that decreases or points past its data is a zuarrow_format_error, and so is a string view outside its buffers in arrow_equal(). Before, arrow_to_r() read past the buffer or raised an unclassed error, and arrow_equal() could crash R (#102).

  • arrow_write() and the decoder that hands a dictionary’s or run-end encoded column’s values to a registered handler check every offset the same way. Before, arrow_write() wrote a batch whose string offsets decrease or point past its data into a file no reader accepts (#150).

  • arrow_read(lazy = TRUE) on a list of sources is lazy: arrow_next() decodes one batch at a time, stream after stream, and frees each source once it is read. Before, every batch was decoded when the handle was made. max_bytes now binds the sources together for paths and connections too, not only for raw vectors (#116).

  • arrow_read() raises zuarrow_type_error for a column position that is infinite or past the integer range. Before, it warned and raised an unclassed error (#125).

  • arrow_write() writes a sliced batch, one with a non-zero offset at any depth, as the values it holds, as arrow, DuckDB and ‘nanoarrow’ slices produce. Every writer failure now has a class: a view layout, a sliced run-end encoded column and a batch with null rows are a zuarrow_type_error, and a malformed batch is a zuarrow_format_error. Before, these raised an unclassed zuarrow_error (#104).

  • arrow_metadata<- raises zuarrow_type_error for a key that is not valid UTF-8 or a value that is not raw. Before, it raised a plain zuarrow_error.

  • A list column of data frames keeps every row of every element; before, its offsets counted columns, not rows, and rows were dropped (#31).

  • Writing a string that is not valid UTF-8, or that is marked as "bytes", is a zuarrow_type_error naming the row. Before, it built an invalid array or raised an unclassed error. Column names are checked the same way (#35).

  • Writing a factor whose code names no level, or whose levels are not strings, is a zuarrow_type_error naming the row, with or without a dictionary (#36).

  • arrow_write() leaves an array it writes usable. Before, it released the caller’s array, so it could not be read or written again (#40).

  • arrow_array() and arrow_stream() no longer set an attribute on the schema handle they are given (#53).

  • Every character column switches to large_utf8 past 2^31 - 1 bytes, including data frame and list columns, and arrow_schema() reports the switch (#52).

  • A list of raw vectors switches to large_binary past 2^31 - 1 bytes, as a character column switches to large_utf8. Before, it was a zuarrow_limit_error. An explicit binary schema still refuses it (#191).

  • A map column converts back to a map. A list with the arrow_keys_sorted attribute is written as map, and a map schema accepts a list of key/value data frames. A null key is a zuarrow_type_error (#41).

  • arrow_equal() compares arrays value by value, as the design says: the bytes under a null slot and the array offset no longer count, and a dictionary or run-end encoded array compares by its decoded values (#64).

  • A dictionary index outside its dictionary is a zuarrow_format_error for every dictionary, not only for factors. Before, a dictionary of numbers read past its end (#50).

  • A factor level with an embedded NUL is cut at the NUL under lossy = "warn" or "allow", as a plain string is, and the lossy error names the dictionary column’s format. Before, it raised an unclassed error (#37).

  • With copy = FALSE, strings inside list elements are copied, as the design says, rather than each element deferring and keeping every batch alive (#55).

  • A decimal with a negative scale round-trips through its text form: the text needs the scale’s trailing zeros, and zero reads as "0" (#54).

  • Registered to handlers apply to the fields of nested data frames at any depth, as documented, and a handled field under a null struct row is NA. Before, only top-level columns used them (#42).

  • An inexact registration may not replace the exact conversion of second and millisecond timestamps, fixed_size_list or the list views (#78).

  • A list column with NULL elements writes to a fixed_size_list, whose null rows still hold their width of child values. Before, it was a zuarrow_type_error, so such a column read from Arrow could not be written back (found by the #48 oracle).

  • arrow_write() computes a null count the producer left unknown (-1) before it writes the batch. Before, the file it wrote could not be read back (#34).

  • Full validation bounds a large list view’s offset plus size without overflowing a 64-bit integer. Before, two large values wrapped around and passed the check, so a hostile IPC input was read out of bounds (#85).

  • arrow_read() refuses a field name or metadata key that holds a NUL or is not valid UTF-8 with a zuarrow_format_error, and so do arrow_metadata() and arrow_to_r() for such a schema. Before, a NUL raised an unclassed error, a NUL in a name cut it short, and invalid bytes became a string marked UTF-8 (#38).

  • A compression level outside the codec’s range, and any codec failure while writing, is a zuarrow_codec_error. Before, it was an unclassed zuarrow_error (#39).

  • arrow_read() finds the size of a file through 64-bit offsets, so a file over 2 GiB opens on Windows (#51).

  • arrow_read() reads a raw vector in place rather than copying it, except with lazy = TRUE, whose handle keeps its own copy (#57).

  • arrow_read() refuses a file whose footer’s copy of the schema differs from its schema message with a zuarrow_format_error. Before, it read the message’s copy, where libarrow reads the footer’s (#33).

  • arrow_read(lazy = TRUE) with to, lossy or copy set is a zuarrow_type_error. Before, it ignored them silently (#78).

  • An unknown lossy, level, format or compression is a zuarrow_type_error, so it inherits from zuarrow_error like every other error. Before, match.arg() raised an unclassed error. The value must now match a choice exactly (#32).

  • arrow_write() raises zuarrow_io_error when it cannot open or write to a path or a connection, and the message keeps the cause, as arrow_read() does. Before, a connection raised unclassed errors and a path lost the cause (#76).

  • as.vector() with a mode other than "any", and as.data.frame() with row.names, are a zuarrow_type_error. Before, both were ignored silently. optional is documented as ignored (#77).

  • The lossy error and warning for a field of a nested data frame that is converted for a registered handler name its path, such as s$b, in the message and in column. Before, they named b alone (#42).

  • Error messages follow one style: “must” for a requirement and “can’t” for what is impossible, one idea per sentence (#80).

  • A list column of functions, environments or calls is a zuarrow_type_error. Before, arrow_schema(list(sum)) recursed until the C stack overflowed (#82).

  • arrow_read() reads a schema nested up to max_depth levels and refuses a deeper one with a zuarrow_limit_error. Before, the bundled FlatBuffers verifier ran out of its own budget from 49 levels, and its failure took time exponential in the depth, so a stream of a few KB, or one written by arrow_write(), stalled the session (#200).

  • arrow_write() writes a field with no name with an empty name, as arrow_read() presents it. Before, an NA column name crashed R (#201).

  • arrow_write() writes metadata values whole. Before, schema, field and extension metadata were cut at the first NUL byte (#202).

  • A stream handle from arrow_read(lazy = TRUE) stays failed after an error: every later arrow_next(), and every later get_next() through the C stream interface, raises the same error. Before, the reader went on to the next message, so a batch was skipped or read against the dictionary that a failed replacement should have replaced (#207).

  • arrow_read() refuses a record batch or dictionary batch whose length differs from its columns’ lengths, as a zuarrow_format_error, as arrow does. Before, a batch shorter than its columns dropped rows silently (#208).

  • arrow_write() writes a batch whose columns are longer than it, as a zero-offset slice of an arrow struct array is, at the batch’s length. Before, each column kept its own length, and arrow refused the output (#206).

  • arrow_write() writes a dictionary whose values hold another dictionary after that inner dictionary, as the format requires. Before, it wrote the outer one first, and arrow_read() refused the output (#186).

  • Running out of memory is a clean error. Failing one allocation could crash R in arrow_read(), arrow_next() and arrow_array(), and could make arrow_write() write a corrupt message without an error. The bundled ‘nanoarrow’ and flatcc code now return the failure (#232).

  • An allocation failure is a bare zuarrow_error, and in arrow_write()’s encoder a zuarrow_limit_error, as design sections 8 and 6.8 say. Before, it could surface as a zuarrow_format_error, zuarrow_handle_error or zuarrow_codec_error, or as a plain R error, so a handler for corrupt input caught it. A stream from any producer that fails with ENOMEM is a bare zuarrow_error too (#233).
